title: Avoiding stalemate: one move mates, one draws
description: White is a queen up and Black's king is in the corner. One careless queen move would throw it all away.
prompt: White to move. Finish the game — carefully.
hints: Before you move, check whether Black would still have a legal move.
Qb6 would take away every square without giving check.

notes.1.Qb7#: Checkmate: the queen on b7 is protected by the king and covers a7 and b8.

explanation: Qb6 would be stalemate: Black's king on a8 would have no legal move but wouldn't be in check, and the game would be a draw. Qb7 gives check, the king on c6 protects the queen, and it's checkmate. When you're winning, always ask: does my opponent still have a move?

source.reference: Avoiding stalemate with king and queen (standard endgame technique); verified with Stockfish 19

title: Avoiding stalemate: give the king a square
description: Black's king has no legal move right now. Almost every quiet move White can make is stalemate.
prompt: White to move. Black's king can't move at all. What does that mean for your next move?
hints: If Black had to move now, it would be stalemate.
Every king move would be stalemate. Give Black's king a square back.

notes.1.Qe7: The queen steps back and gives Black's king the square g8 — no stalemate.

explanation: Black's king on h8 has no legal move. Kg6 or Kh6 would be stalemate — in fact every king move would be. First give the king a square with Qe7; after Kg8, Kg6 brings White's king closer and Qf8 is mate. A winning player has to keep the opponent breathing until the very last move.

source.reference: Avoiding stalemate with king and queen (standard endgame technique); verified with Stockfish 19

title: The early queen loses time
description: White brings the queen out on move two. Black develops and attacks it again and again.

notes.2.Qh5: The queen comes out on move two.
notes.3...g6: The pawn attacks the queen, which has to move.
notes.5...Nd4: The knight attacks the queen on b3 and the pawn on c2.
notes.6...c6: Black is ready to push the b-pawn, and White's queen is running out of squares.

explanation: White's queen moved four times in the first six moves: g6 and Nd4 attacked it, and every time it had to move, Black developed with gain of time. After six moves Black has both knights out and White is clearly worse. Develop your knights and bishops first; the queen comes later.

source.reference: opening principle; Stockfish 19: White +0.22 before 2.Qh5, -2.77 at the end

title: Moving the same bishop again and again
description: White's bishop moves four times, and every move gives Black a free pawn move forward.

notes.3.Bb5: The bishop moves a second time.
notes.4...b5: Again: the b-pawn attacks the bishop on a4.
notes.7...e4: The pawn attacks the knight on f3.
notes.8...Bc5: Black develops with an attack on the knight on d4.

explanation: White's bishop went c4-b5-a4-b3: four moves, each answered by a black pawn move that gained space. Now Black has a big pawn centre, chases White's knight as well and develops with gain of time. Move each piece once, to a good square, before moving any piece again.

source.reference: opening principle; Stockfish 19: White -0.01 before 3.Bb5, -1.60 at the end

title: Edge pawns instead of development
description: White plays pawn moves on the edge of the board. Black develops and castles.

notes.2.h3: Another edge pawn move: no piece comes out.
notes.6...O-O: Black has three pieces out and has castled; White has developed one bishop.

explanation: White spent five of six moves on pawn moves, four of them at the edge of the board. Black used the same time to take the centre, bring out three pieces and castle. In the opening, put pawns in the centre and get your knights and bishops out.

source.reference: opening principle; Stockfish 19: White -0.18 before 2.h3, -1.44 at the end
